notes:
I've written notes on Mark 14:25–48 below, organised by verse with a link after each point. A few things to know first:

- **Several verses are thin.** The full Enduring Word, Precept Austin and Barclay pages cut off before reaching these verses, and the Constable page wouldn't load. Much of the material comes from search excerpts. I found nothing usable for vv. 27–28 on the Zechariah quote or the promise about Galilee.
- **No denominational splits came up.** No Pentecostal, Lutheran, Methodist (Wesley's note on v. 47 gives only cross-references) or Orthodox commentary on these verses turned up, and no netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org notes. Where I mention a disagreement, it's a difference between individual teachers, not between traditions.
- **The searches didn't surface any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on these verses.** Where a commentator labels a source by tradition, I say so. Otherwise I don't guess.

---

**v. 25**
- John Gill reads "drink it new" figuratively, as the joys of heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/14-25.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary links it to the regeneration of all things. Disciples who now feed on Christ in the sacrament and by faith will then eat at His table in His kingdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/14-25.htm
- Constable sees Jesus anticipating the messianic banquet at the beginning of His kingdom (cf. Isaiah 25:6), a comfort after the announcement of His death. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-25.html
- **Differing views:** *Contending for the Faith* (labelled Restoration Movement) notes that some think this "day" means Pentecost, when Christ would eat with His disciples "in spirit" at the Lord's Supper. It prefers the view that the verse refers to the time after the resurrection. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-25.html
- A Bible Hub Q&A article ties the verse to the Passover's fourth cup and calls it a pledge of a literal, joyous banquet after His return. That article openly works within a young-earth, millennial framework. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_drink_it_new_in_Mark_14_25.htm
- Matthew Henry says the Supper was meant to remain in force till his second coming. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/14-25.htm
- *The Bible Says* puts it simply: the Supper looks back to the sacrifice and forward to Christ's return. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/mar-14-v22-25.cfm

**v. 26**
- Lane (quoted by Guzik) says Psalm 118 was on Jesus' lips as He went to Gethsemane. The psalm describes God guiding the Messiah through suffering to glory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/
- Hamilton Smith says singing a hymn on the way to betrayal and agony shows a calm that came from keeping the Father's will and the joy beyond the cross in view. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hsw/mark-14.html

**vv. 27–28**
- Hiebert notes that Mark and Matthew place the warning on the way to Gethsemane, but Luke and John record it in the upper room. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary
- Constable thinks the prediction was made in the upper room, and that Mark placed it here because it connects logically with the arrest. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-14.html
- Guzik instead reconstructs two warnings: one in the upper room and another on the way to Gethsemane. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/

**v. 29**
- MacArthur says Peter had seen so much of Christ's power that he felt sure he could withstand anything while Jesus was there. That confidence showed again in the garden. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary
- Spurgeon's sermon notes list Peter's boast as one of the things Peter later remembered with grief. He asks readers whether they too have broken earnest promises. https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons_sermon_notes-mark

**vv. 30–31**
- Wessel says the story warned a persecuted church: if an apostle could deny Christ, so could they. It also assured them that repentance and restoration were possible. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary
- Spurgeon notes that Peter later remembered he had been solemnly forewarned by his Lord, and remembered his own vows. https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons_sermon_notes-mark

**v. 32**
- "Gethsemane" means "oil press" or "olive press," a fitting name for where Jesus would be pressed hard. Guzik adds: the Son of God would be crushed here. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary
- Barclay says staying in the upper room was risky. Judas knowing to look in Gethsemane shows Jesus went there habitually. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/mark-14.html
- Spurgeon (quoted on Precept Austin) says Jesus went there not to hide from death but to prepare for it by prayer. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary
- J. C. Ryle sees Jesus, sinless as He was, setting an example of constant prayer. https://www.preceptaustin.org/j-c-ryle-gospel-of-mark-commentary
- The exact site is uncertain. Brooks notes there are now Latin, Armenian, Greek Orthodox and Russian Orthodox "Gethsemanes." https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary

**v. 33**
- A. T. Robertson says the Greek word means Jesus Himself felt amazement as He faced the struggle. Swete adds that when the Passion came into view, its terror exceeded His anticipations. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary
- Guzik says the cause was not fear of physical torture but the spiritual horror of being made sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/
- Constable sees the scene contrasting Jesus' dependence on the Father with Peter's self-confidence. He calls it a remarkable revelation of the humanity of Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-14.html

**v. 34**
- Coffman says Satan, beaten in the wilderness, now returned with all his human servants. He quotes Barth: "The bill was being presented!" https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/mark-14.html
- Spurgeon's notes say Jesus asked for His friends' sympathy, even though, like Him, we may find such support feeble. https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons_sermon_notes-mark
- The *Church Pulpit Commentary* says Gethsemane explains Jesus' calm silence at His trials. It was needed to strengthen His moral nature for what followed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/mark-14.html

**v. 35**
- People usually prayed standing. The weight of the moment drove Jesus to His knees (Luke) and then onto His face (Matthew). https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary
- Coffman says it became clear in the garden that Christ's death could not be avoided without abandoning the whole plan of salvation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/mark-14.html
- On "the hour," James Edwards says Jesus is not a tragic hero caught in events beyond his control. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary

**v. 36**
- **"Abba":** Guzik calls it a child's familiar word for "daddy." Precept Austin's word note explains it more carefully: an Aramaic form meaning "the Father," which came to mean "My Father." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary
- **"The cup":** Guzik says the Father didn't remove the cup but strengthened Jesus to drink it, the cup of the Father's fury. Akin says Jesus drank the cup of wrath so that we might drink the cup of salvation. Guzik also says the prayer rules out any other way of salvation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary
- **Where teachers differ — was Gethsemane part of the atonement?**
  - Guzik says the struggle of the cross was won in the garden. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/
  - The Precept Austin compiler and William MacDonald disagree. MacDonald says redemption was accomplished during the three hours of darkness on the cross, and Gethsemane was in anticipation of Calvary. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary
- **How far did Jesus feel forsaken?**
  - Guzik says Jesus was treated, as it were, as an enemy of God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/
  - The *Expositor's Bible* finds it incredible that Jesus suffered estrangement like that of lost souls. It holds that He took our place but still prayed to God as Father. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/mark-14.html
- **One will or two?** Ironside (quoted by Guzik) says "there was no conflict of wills." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/
  - The historic answer, shared across traditions, is that Christ has a divine will and a human will. The Third Council of Constantinople (680–681) affirmed this. Monergism (Reformed) argues that without a true human will, His obedience in Gethsemane could not stand in our place as the Second Adam. https://www.monergism.com/topics/jesus-christ/incarnation/dyothelitism
  - GotQuestions says the council taught that the two wills are not contrary to each other. https://www.gotquestions.org/dyotheletism.html
  - Catholic Answers gives the traditional Catholic reading: His human will faced the natural human dread of death and freely submitted to the divine will. It defends this against a modern critic referred to as Craig, who thinks the council got it wrong. https://www.catholic.com/audio/sp/why-i-dont-believe-in-sola-scriptura
- **"If it be Your will":** Guzik answers the claim that a prayer like this insults God. If it did, he says, Jesus insulted His Father in the garden. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/
  - Hastings' *Great Texts* says bluntly Christ's prayer did not succeed, meaning He didn't get what He asked for. Hastings also says God was as near in Gethsemane as at the Transfiguration. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hastings/mark/14-36.htm

**v. 37**
- Guzik says Jesus wasn't irritated but spoke in love. Calling Peter "Simon" pointed to his old self. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/

**v. 38**
- Guzik says watching and praying could have kept Peter from denying Jesus. The spiritual battle is often won or lost before the crisis comes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/
- Precept Austin says Peter's tests showed he could not resist temptation in his own strength, and we need God's grace just as constantly. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary
- The *Expositor's Bible* says Gethsemane shows that every part of human nature may be heard, as long as the spirit has the final say. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/mark-14.html

**v. 39**
- Guzik says some call repeated prayers unspiritual, yet Jesus repeated His. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/
- Precept Austin suggests Scripture records only part of what He prayed. It sees His prayer as an example for our own "Gethsemane" moments. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary

**vv. 40–41**
- Guzik says the disciples slept each of the three times. They should have prayed for Jesus' sake as well as their own. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/
- G. Campbell Morgan reads "sleep on" as kindly: Jesus let them sleep and kept watch Himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/
- Constable notes Mark's threes: three returns, three denials, three questions from Pilate. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-14.html
  - Both Jesus and Peter faced a threefold temptation. Jesus won and Peter fell, and the difference goes back to Gethsemane. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-14.html

**v. 42**
- Edwards stresses that Jesus does not cower or retreat but stays in control of events. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary

**v. 43**
- A writer quoted on Precept Austin says Judas broke into his Master's place of prayer on the most sacred night of the Passover. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary
- Guzik suggests the mob may have gone first to Mark's family home, where the upper room may have been. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/

**vv. 44–45**
- Guzik says Judas had to identify Jesus because He looked ordinary. Judas faked affection with his kiss and greeting. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/
- Barclay translates it as a kiss as a lover would. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-47.html
- R. C. Sproul says God did not force Judas; Judas did what he wanted, and God brought redemption out of the betrayal. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary
- MacArthur calls Judas history's great example of wasted privilege. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-14-commentary

**v. 46**
- Matthew Henry pictures rough, violent hands, and the captors likely gloating that they'd finally done what they had often tried. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-47.html
- Ellicott renders "took him" as "seized." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-47.html

**v. 47**
- The Pulpit Commentary says only John names the swordsman (Peter) and the servant (Malchus); only Luke records the healing. https://biblehub.com/mark/14-47.htm
- The Cambridge Bible notes a view that the other Gospels left out Peter's name to protect him from revenge. It suggests the ear may not have been fully cut off. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/14-47.htm
- Barclay agrees it wasn't yet safe to name Peter. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-47.html
- **Commentators judge Peter's act differently:**
  - Barclay is half-approving: there was one man ready to strike a blow for Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-47.html
  - The *Preacher's Homiletical Commentary* is critical: Christian heroism endures, and does not smite. Glover calls all religious violence by inquisitors "Peter's mistake." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-47.html
  - Guzik says worldly power in Peter's hands could only cut off ears. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/
  - Matthew Henry thinks Peter aimed for the head. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-47.html
  - Barclay (quoted by Guzik) notes that without the healing there might have been four crosses at Calvary. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/

**v. 48**
- The *Preacher's Homiletical Commentary* says the question asserts Jesus' innocence and His captors' guilt, and shows force is useless against Him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-47.html
- Matthew Henry says the weapons were meant to make Jesus look dangerous and turn the people against Him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/14-47.html
- Guzik says Jesus marvelled at the armed crowd, yet was the one in command. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-14/
